questions.q: What do DevOps interviewers typically look for first when they open a candidate's GitHub profile?
options: The total number of repositories
A long daily commit streak
A README that explains the architecture and reasoning quickly, plus real commit history
The number of GitHub followers
questions.explain: Interviewers care about whether the README communicates the system clearly and whether the commit history shows real iterative work, not vanity metrics like repo count or streaks.

questions.q: Why should the 'design decisions' section be added to a portfolio README?
options: It makes the README longer, which looks more thorough
It answers 'walk me through a decision you made' before the interviewer asks
It is required by GitHub
It replaces the need for a working application
questions.explain: A design decisions section preemptively explains why choices like remote state locking or differentiated autoscaling were made, turning the README into an interview artifact.

questions.q: For a monorepo like northbridgeretail/storefront, what should be pinned on a GitHub profile?
options: Only the checkout service folder
The entire monorepo, so the top-level layout is visible
A screenshot of the repo instead of the repo itself
Nothing — monorepos shouldn't be made public
questions.explain: Pinning the whole monorepo lets a reviewer see services/, infra/terraform/, charts/, and .github/workflows/ at a glance, which communicates platform understanding better than a single folder.

questions.q: Why is running gitleaks against only the current working tree insufficient before open-sourcing a repo?
options: gitleaks only works on private repos
A secret removed in a later commit can still exist in earlier commits in git history
The working tree is always clean by default
gitleaks cannot scan Terraform or Helm files
questions.explain: Deleting a secret in a new commit doesn't remove it from git history; a scan must cover history, not just the current tree, or rewrite history to actually remove it.

questions.q: Before publishing a capstone-style repo that resembles real employer work, what should a candidate do?
options: Nothing extra — fictional company names make it automatically safe
Get written permission if any of the work is based on actual employer infrastructure
Publish immediately to build a portfolio faster
Only scrub secrets, infrastructure names don't matter
questions.explain: Even with fictional names, if underlying work reflects real employer infrastructure or decisions, written permission should be obtained before making it public.
